::: {.bs-editorial-lead}
NICE is useful only if students can move through it, test an idea, discover something new, and return to earlier decisions.
:::

## N: Needs and Necessities

Students begin by identifying what a solution must do and what would make it better. Needs should include a minimum acceptable condition. Necessities can be prioritized so trade-offs become visible.

## I: Investigate and Inquire

Investigation turns assumptions into questions. Students gather measurements, examples, constraints, references, observations, and possible approaches before committing to a solution.

## C: Create and Communicate

Creation includes more than fabrication. Sketches, code, CAD, schematics, prototypes, calculations, tests, and explanations all help turn an idea into something that can be examined and discussed.

## E: Evaluate

Evaluation compares the result with the original needs and necessities. Evidence from testing should identify what worked, what failed, what changed, and what should happen next.

## Back to N

The important step is returning to Needs and Necessities. Evaluation may reveal that a requirement was incomplete, unrealistic, poorly measured, or no longer important. The next cycle begins with better information than the first.

That is why Technology Commons treats NICE as `N -> I -> C -> E -> N`, not as a four-box checklist that ends when a project is submitted.
